extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, fiction writers, and storytellers seeking craft guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles for designing story structure, scenes, characters, and the inciting incident; focused on creating dynamic beats, authentic worlds, and a unifying spine of desire. Geared to writers (particularly screenwriters) crafting dramatic fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Gap (substance of story)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of story is the gap that splits open between what a human being expects to happen when he takes an action and what really does happen; the rift between expectation and result, probability and necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build scenes by repeatedly breaking open breaches between expectation and result; the audience empathizes when the gap opens, producing emotional reactions ('Oh, my God!', 'Oh, no!', 'Oh, yes!'). The gap is also the source of story energy; each turn forces characters to pour more energy into their next action and makes the audience feel surges of energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create within the gap (inner monologue technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put inner monologues into 'ultra-slow motion' on the page: give words to flights of feeling or flashes of insight that on screen take minutes or seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settle into a character's conscious center and ask 'If I were this character in these circumstances, what would I do?' Then step out to take an objective look at the action created and pry open the opposing reaction. Writing may take days or weeks to render minutes on screen; be patient and meticulous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift points of view to open gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not remain locked in a single character's point of view; move around the universe to another point of view (even inanimate) to create unexpected reactions and splinter the cleft between expectation and result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After creating an honest moment from one POV, invade another POV, then return to the first to find a new emotional truth under changed circumstances. Repeated shifting yields successive action/reaction/gap beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine writing emphasizes reactions: less stress on what happens than on to whom it happens, why, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build scenes beat by beat as action → reaction → gap; reactions should provide insight and imagination. The richest pleasures come from focusing on characters' reactions and the psychological consequence of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'pointless pace killers' (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'pointless pace killer' is any scene where reactions lack insight and imagination so expectation equals result, producing dead seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will cut such scenes. Example anti-pattern: a character knocks and the door is politely opened—this wastes time and stalls pace. Ensure each beat generates surprise, conflict, or deeper revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid, experiential description
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a vivid description of what happens and the reactions it gets so that readers live through the roller coaster of life beat by beat, gap by gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe what is seen, said, and done with enough specificity that a reader's pulse pounds and emotions flow. Use language that allows readers to plunge into each gap and feel the writer's insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy of story derives from the gap
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of energy in story is the gap; as it opens for character it opens for the audience, producing visceral physical responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design turns that increase pressure on characters so audience empathy accumulates as energy through the narrative; each beat should raise stakes and exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident must be dynamic and fully developed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inciting Incident is the first major event of the telling and the primary cause for all that follows; it must be a dynamic, fully developed event, not something static or vague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Inciting Incident must radically upset the balance of forces in the protagonist's life. Anti-example: a vague move to another city without consequential stakes. Good Inciting Incidents create immediate, perceivable imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident can require setup + payoff but payoff cannot be delayed
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally an Inciting Incident needs two events (setup and payoff); if so, the payoff cannot be delayed too long while keeping the protagonist ignorant of the imbalance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: JAWS — setup (shark eats swimmer), payoff (sheriff discovers corpse). Avoid designs that withhold the payoff and interpose irrelevant episodic scenes (anti-pattern illustrated by THE RIVER).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident upsets balance (negative or positive)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a story begins the protagonist has relative control; an Inciting Incident swings the value-charge of the protagonist's reality either to the negative or the positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative and positive incidents both must create pressure: either danger, loss, or new responsibility. The protagonist must become aware that life is out of balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must react to the Inciting Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist must respond to the sudden change in balance in a way appropriate to character and world; even refusal to act is a reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal can be a valid reaction but cannot endure too long; ultimately the protagonist is aroused to restore balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident produces Object of Desire and propels action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inciting Incident arouses in the protagonist a desire to restore equilibrium and leads to conception of an Object of Desire: something he lacks that will set things right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Out of this need the protagonist actively pursues the Object of Desire, which in many stories is sufficient to carry the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious vs unconscious desire (depth of character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex protagonists have both conscious and unconscious desires; the unconscious desire often contradicts the conscious one and drives inner conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the interplay/contradiction between conscious and unconscious desires to create layered, morally and psychologically complex characters (examples: CARNAL KNOWLEDGE, MRS. SOFFEL, THE CRYING GAME).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spine of the story (through-line / super-objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spine is the deep desire in and effort by the protagonist to restore the balance of life. It's the primary unifying force that holds all story elements together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every scene, image, and word should causally or thematically relate to the Spine. If the unconscious desire drives the story, it becomes the Spine; otherwise the conscious objective serves as Spine (e.g., Bond).

rubrics_metrics.name: If no unconscious desire, conscious objective becomes Spine
rubrics_metrics.description: When a protagonist lacks an unconscious desire, his conscious objective becomes the Spine of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such stories can be straightforward (example: James Bond — to defeat the arch-villain); maintain consistency of the protagonist's pursuit or the story will collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity over actuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity means an internally consistent world, true to itself in scope, depth, and detail; a convincing impossibility is preferable to an unconvincing possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and selected details must persuade the audience to willingly suspend disbelief. Authenticity concerns believability within the story's own rules, not factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial knowledge: author = authority = authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: A true author is an artist with godlike knowledge of his subject; the proof of authorship is that his pages 'smack of authority' and produce authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive research and mastery of subject let a writer choose exactly what to stress and what to lay down subtly; authority engenders audience trust and empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research setting deeply (period, duration, location, level of conflict)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is defined in terms of period, duration, location, and level of conflict; fill that frame with depth and breadth of detail to avoid clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research to generate unique atmosphere and personality for the story; ask detailed questions to saturate your knowledge of the world before inventing events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question characters' work life (useful moments only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how characters make a living and understand their day-to-day work; most work is boring and should be shown only when it causes problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In professional genres (Courtroom, Crime, Medical), focus scenes on moments when work creates complications; to get inside character, examine full 24-hour life (work, play, love, prayer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine politics/power in the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the orchestration of power (politics) in any social structure—families, corporations, institutions—and how people gain or lose power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even household dynamics are political; identify who wields power and how it shifts (patriarchal, matriarchal, kid-tyrannized). Politics provides conflict and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rituals and daily rites matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the rituals of your world—public ceremonies and private rites—that structure characters' lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ritual details (how people sit, dress, observe habits) reveal character and authenticity. Small infractions of ritual can create meaningful friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eating/mealtime rituals
rubrics_metrics.description: How characters take meals is a revealing ritual—who eats where, how, and what this implies socially and culturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mealtime scenes to show social patterns, status, and relationships (e.g., dressing for dinner vs open-fridge contemporary habits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Values: moral and legal distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask what characters consider good/evil or right/wrong, and what they see as worth living or dying for; legal/moral categories may not align.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values drive choices and conflicts; clarify societal laws and belief systems to create credible motivations and dilemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backstory (precise definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Backstory is the set of significant events that occurred in characters' pasts which the writer can use to build the story's progressions; it's not mere biography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use backstory as a reservoir for creating causal progressions; plant events deliberately that will be harvested during the story rather than dumping biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast design and polarization
rubrics_metrics.description: Every role must fit a purpose; the first principle of cast design is polarization—devising a network of contrasting or contradictory attitudes among roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each character reacts distinctively to events; if two characters react identically, collapse them into one or remove one. Polarization maximizes opportunities for conflict and scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling detail (selective specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity depends on the 'telling detail': using a few selected details allows the audience's imagination to supply the rest and complete a credible whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overdoing realism, especially with sex and violence—too much explicitness can shatter credibility. Trust small, resonant details rather than exhaustive literalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality arises from authenticity, not eccentricity
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal style is the spontaneous effect of an author mastering subject and resisting clichés; originality comes from authentic choices rather than forced eccentricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let authorial knowledge meet personality naturally; study exemplars to see how different authors' knowledge/temperament produce distinct voices (e.g., Waldo Salt vs Alvin Sargent).
